One thing a lot of people tend to forget is that when discussing a 'structural deficit' there is also the concept of a 'structural surplus'.... and Canada hasn't really had a structural surplus of note since about 2003. In 2004 Canada broke even. We had a tiny surplus, but for all intents and purposes that is the year that the structural surplus was eliminated. For 2005 through 2007 we probably would have been in a deficit if it hadn't been for an extremely strong world-wide economy during those two years. Even if Harper hadn't changed anything we probably would have had about a $20B deficit in 2009. However since we cut taxes by about $10B/year and increased spending by $25B/year we instead had a deficit of $55B.In a few years we'll be back to where we were in 2004 in terms of spending vs. tax revenue (in what might be surprising to some, both are expected to be at about the same level vs. GDP as they were in 2004). If we do reach that point we should be at the stage of no structural deficit and also no structural surplus. In other words, if the world-wide economy is doing well we'll run surpluses, if it is doing poorly we'll run deficits.

The 'CO2 is plant food' argument is an old one. It works in greenhouses usually, but it doesn't seem to work so well in natural settings where the same factors that increase CO2 also increase ozone and temperatures and decrease water and nitrogen availability. It's a complicated area of research. You end up with crops with more leaf matter but fewer nutrients, or ones that don't have normal disease resistance, or ones that have inadequate roots to hold up their above ground parts. It all depends on the type of plant, the type of photosynthesis it uses (C3/C4/CAM), peak temperatures, and especially on how much warmer it gets on average (plants grow better up to a certain threshold and then they just choke). Start here: www.skepticalscience.com/co2-plant-food.htmAnd then try here: Current evidence suggests that that the concentrations of atmospheric CO2 predicted for the year 2100 will have major implications for plant physiology and growth. Under elevated CO2 most plant species show higher rates of photosynthesis, increased growth, decreased water use and lowered tissue concentrations of nitrogen and protein. Rising CO2 over the next century is likely to affect both agricultural production and food quality. The effects of elevated CO2 are not uniform; some species, particularly those that utilize the C4 variant of photosynthesis, show less of a response to elevated CO2 than do other types of plants. Rising CO2 is therefore likely to have complex effects on the growth and composition of natural plant communities. www.nature.com/scitable/knowledge/library/effects-of-rising-atmospheric-concentrations-of-carbon-13254108A thought experiment ... oxygen-is-people-foodIf I increase your oxygen levels, how much more do think you would grow, or would have grown if you're all grown already? @Dr Strangelove... the ocean is a complex 3-D volume and there are indeed numerous mechanisms for excess heat storage and release (mainly at the sea surface, but all over the world at almost all possible temperatures) as well as internal redistribution. The oceans on average are warm near the surface and cold at depth. This implies a constant heat transport downwards... yet somehow the deep ocean remains cold. This is because the deep waters can also lose (and gain) heat directly at the sea surface... with transport and exchange taking place 'laterally' (roughly along layers of constant density) from sea-surface regions at higher latitudes. So let's imagine an insulated rod that has one end maintained at 20 C, and which is stuck into a bucket of ice at its other end. There is a temperature gradient along the rod. Now take the one end of the rod out of the ice, but keep the other end at 20 C. The cold end of the rod warms, but the warm end stays at 20 C. the overall heat content of the rod increases until the temperature gradient disappears. Of course this is not even close to how the real, complex ocean or ocean heat storage works... but it is an analogy to the fact that the ocean exchanges heat not only at its 'warm end' but also at its 'cold end'... and so it is possible to store heat in the deep (cold) ocean while keeping the heat content of the warm part of the ocean more or less the same... So in a sense, and following your analogy, the excess heat does not need to take a downward escalator.. it could hitch a ride along the long, almost horizontal conveyor belt which extending from the sea surface at high latitudes to the deep ocean interior... Not saying any of this is simple... or even understood right now in great detail. I'd certainly agree with 'climate skeptics' who say that we need more accurate measurement of ocean heat storage.. and an improved understanding of how the deep ocean works as part of the climate system.

There's a lot of talk these days - especially by people who'd like to introduce a 2-tier medical system to Canada - about how foul our healthcare setup is.As a person who has had close family members and friends treated for either life-threatening or terminal disease in the course of the past 15 years, I have found that for the most part everyone received excellent and timely care, with amazing doctors and specialists, and top-notch facilities. I am not saying that for day-to-day health concerns, or when going for your annual checkup, etc. there aren't glitches in the system. It can be terribly frustrating. There is no question that we should find more efficiencies. Perhaps people should pay fees for showing up for annual checkups and minor complaints (like colds, which no doctor can treat anyway). Administration should be streamlined. There should be more nurse practitioners. People who want warts removed (or similar minor ailments) should not have to be referred to a 'specialist'. And so on.But I would not endorse a two-tier system of private care for some, and free care for the poor. This would lead us ultimately to the American system, where if you have the money you get the best care it can buy, and where you don't... you don't. And if you're part of the middle class and dealing with serious illness - of the sort my family and friends in past years - you can be made a pauper trying to pay, since the system doesn't consider you 'poor' enough to get the services for free.

There is no evidence that cannabis legalization will increase usage rates. According the Supreme Court of Canada, usage rates 'rise and fall with no apparent statistical relationship to cannabis laws and their enforcement.' We know this from comparing jurisdictions with differing penalties and levels of enforcement, and by tracking changes before and after penalties and enforcement are relaxed or ratcheted up. North American teens are twice as likely to use cannabis as Dutch teens. Tobacco smoking rates have been dropping for decades. Canadian teens are more likely to graduate from high school having tried cannabis than tobacco, and they report that cannabis is easier to obtain than beer. What really controls usage rates, and prevents use from becoming abuse, is education, treatment and harm reduction. Prohibition impedes all of these proven public health interventions. It drives a wedge between doctors and patients, parents and children, teachers and students and the police and their communities. Moreover, we spend about 70 per cent of our drug control budget on enforcement and corrections, 17 per cent on treatment, 5 per cent on prevention and 2 per cent on harm reduction. To the extent money formerly wasted on prohibition is re-allocated to public health interventions, usage rates, and what harm cannabis causes, will be held in check. There is every reason to believe that, after an initial spike, once the novelty has worn off, usage rates will go down, and certainly the harm caused by cannabis will go down as consumers shift to extracts, edibles and vaporizers and strains of known potency and purity, and more likely to contain closer CBD/THC ratios. Smoking is not everyone's cup of tea. That puts a natural cap on the number of potential cannabis smokers. Alcohol, being a beverage, doesn't have this cap. The high from cannabis is qualitatively different than the high from chardonnay. Alcohol disinhibits, which makes it great for dinner parties and dates. The high from cannabis is not to everyone's taste, which puts another cap on the number of potential users. Consider that few people huff gasoline, despite widespread availability. Cannabis rivals lumber and wheat as Canada's most lucrative cash crop. Although big business produces alcohol and tobacco products, they don't have a monopoly on them. I prefer beer from local micro breweries. Wine production is also widely diversified between small vineyards and big companies. Cannabis connoisseurs, like beer and wine connoisseurs, are willing to pay more for quality and variety. Finally, cannabis is an economic substitute for alcohol and other drugs, with cross-price elasticities, meaning, when cannabis use goes up, drinking and other drug use goes does, causing a net reduction in DUI traffic accidents, crime, violence, homicides, suicides, rape, domestic abuse, unplanned pregnancies, overdose deaths, FASD, disease and addiction.

Despite all the faults people may find with Reg 274, it moves the TDSB from a destructive and deeply inefficient hiring system to a process where teachers a) graduate with no experience, b) then get some daily supply experience, c) then do some LTOs and get some teaching experience, d) then apply for permanent positions. The so-called ?old teachers with the seniority? in this discussion are not teachers who have been working for the TDSB for 20 years. They are teachers who graduated from teachers college perhaps 3 or 5 or 8 years ago and have been cobbling together a teaching career ever since, doing a few months here and a few months there. There is a large group of TDSB ?supply teachers? who have been doing ?full time? teaching, covering for maternity and extended illness leaves, and teaching full course loads for full semesters (LTOs). These teachers are ?new,? but not ?brand-new-with-no-experience-direct-from-college.? If ever there was a group of teachers whose members had proved their mettle, it is this group. These teachers have been hired again and again to do ?real full time teaching? (LTOs) by principals?principals who could hire anyone they wanted from the entire supply teaching list, and chose these teachers based on other principals? references. In other words, hired them on the merit of their real world in-classroom experience. Lost in the furor over Reg 274 forcing principals to hire for LTOs from a restricted pool is the fact that before 274 principals had to hire PERMANENT POSITIONS from a restricted pool--in that case it was the pool of teachers on the Eligible to Hire list (ETH). The ETH list was a board-level-managed (i.e., not principals) black-box; how people did or didn't get on that list was opaque, byzantine, and deeply corrupt. Principals were restricted to hiring from that ETH pool, and REGULARLY in MANY cases were prevented from hiring the teacher that they wanted: the teacher that they had hired to do a semester-long LTO, that they had seen and evaluated in the classroom, that fit the school culture, etc etc, and that now they wanted to hire for a permanent position. If that teacher was not on the ETH--and often they were not, since doing LTOs and being on the ETH were unrelated--the principal was irrevocably blocked from hiring the teacher. In the farther past, 5+ years ago, principals had the power to make a call and have a teacher 'put on the ETH' but that power was removed. Populating the ETH was done purely at board-level and with no transparency or oversight. All the seniority issues could be stripped out of 274 and it would still be a vast improvement on the old TDSB ETH hiring system that was demonstrably bad for students and hated by principals, teachers, and unions alike. The only people who liked the ETH were the group of queue-jumping fresh grads each year. (And, presumably, by the people who had the power to control what teachers were added to the ETH.)

Rather than 'income splitting', what should be getting discussed is 'income pooling' for an entire family, with a simple flat tax on the total pool. Income tax was supposed to be an interim, temporary measure to pay for the war. Instead, the corporate tax burden got shifted on the middle class, and the income tax act just gets more and more convoluted, virtually ensuring that regular people will overpay their share of the taxes. Only the wealthy can afford to hire the high priced tax attorneys to help them evade the onerous tax burden enforced by the government. Here's the solution, as I see it. Every Canadian gets a basic personal exemption that is sufficient to fund a 'poverty line' standard of living. No taxes on any income earned below that level. Then, an appropriate flat tax - one percentage for all - is applied to every dollar over that basic personal exemption amount. And, of course, if corporations want to be treated as people, then they should be treated as people in all regards including this one. No need for tax lawyers, no loopholes for the rich, just a fair tax regime for all.

About an era only 16 years old, Liz Renzetti, a journalist I admire, writes: 'we tended to let demi-truths pass by in those days.' Not really. Scotland's independence movement is driven by both cultural and economic motivations. There is a belief that they'd be better off economically on their own; or at the very least they'd be able to maintain a standard of living while providing more opportunities for Scots to stay in Scotland, as opposed to have to emigrate to other parts of the UK or the globe for good jobs. Scotland, mind you, is home to much of the UK's oil reserves in the North Sea... and we know what Alberta would be like if most of the wealth from their oil went to Toronto. Right? Rae's point that London is a bit late to the game on listening to Scotland's grievances is spot on. The big loser will be England, who has benefited from using Scotland for a long time.

Universities are not like corporations and professors are not mid-level managers in a corporate hierarchy. And nor should they be - universities serve a much different social purpose and serve a public rather than a private interest.

GM apple could cross-pollinate with organic and traditional apple resulting in GM contamination. Organic producers could lose their certification and conventional growers could lose their reputation worlwide. Okanagan valley where about 98 percent of BC apples are produced and where the GM apple trees would be planted this could mean substantial revenue loss for producers. Seeds from GM apples could also cause the growth of new GM trees (anywhere in the world) through seed droping. Finally browning in apples is easily delayed with lemon juice and there are already naturally slow-browning apple like the BC Ambrosia.

Our Grade 9 home-room class was held each morning in the Junior High's Home Economics classroom, so, unlike other students, we all sat around about 8 big, rectangular wooden tables, enjoying an intimacy and closeness students in other classrooms didn't experience. Wallace Parker was one of about 8 kids who sat at my table. Wally was what we, in those days, called an 'Indian,' a big, soft-spoken, smiling, laughing kid we all liked. If my religion does not allow me to sit next to another person on the basis of sex, I am responsible for ensuring that the seat adjacent to me is not occupied by a person of the offending sex. It's not just that it's all right for a woman to feed her child; it's that it's NOT all right to ask her to cover up. Legitimate matters of religious accommodation should be restricted to allowing people to do things that affect THEM, and never things that affect others.

One of the most well-understood flaws of First-past-the-post is that it is majoritarian. When Canada was established there were a number of constraints placed on the commons to minimise the impact of this flaw - the upper chamber to represent minority interests, the Queen to be able to overrule the majority, the prime ministers power was relatively limited as an executive. All of these have broken down - the senate is coopted by the parties of the commons, the queens representative would never step in, and the prime minister has become presidential in power. Trudeau is working to undo some of these things - distance between commons and senate, proportional voting to reduce the power of the majority, etc. I think the best argument for why reform is needed is the fact that Trudeau didn't need to consult the opposition to change voting, he could have forced a Liberal majority on the committee and jammed through the legislation. Referendums are even worse forms of majoritarian rule. The suggestion that we should rely on tyranny of the majority to solve the problem of tyranny of the majority is nonsensical.

Professor Kingwell himself seems to run together truth or fact with knowledge, evidence, and what it is warranted or rational to believe on the evidence, Truth isn't falsifiable or corrigible, but what we are warranted on the evidence in believing to be true may be. That's why innocent people can be found guilty ---George in fact did not kill Harry even though he is found guilty of doing so---and, on the basis of the evidence available at the time to the jury, it may even be beyond a reasonable doubt to the jury that he is guilty. That is also why why what it is reasonable for scientists to believe at one time to be true on the basis of the evidence may not be reasonable for them to believe to be true on the basis of new evidence or theoretical developments. Running these distinctions together itself helps contribute to the post-factual, post-evidential world. As Professor Kingwell suggests,, enthusiasm, fanaticism, and the lust for power have long undermined any concern for truth or what the evidence warrants one in believing to be true. We could cite Hitler or Stalin or the Protocols of the Elders of Zion. However, a less stock and less emotionally loaded example is the famous, fraudulent ' Donation of Constantine' , forged by medieval monks to be used by the medieval Church to support its claims to spiritual and temporal authority. The forgery itself was established only in the 15th century by Renaissance humanists using philological evidence,, but the fact that the forgery came to be fairly well recognized as proven, even in the Church itself apart from a few holdouts, buttresses Professor Kingwell's view that the disregard for truth and evidence in the contemporary world may be something different.. So what is the difference? Here Professor Kingwell isn?t very helpful, but it is surprising that he doesn?t bother to mention the role of post-modernism and post-modernist theory in the humanities and social sciences over the past 30 years---apart that is to say, from analytic philosophy departments and analytical philosophers of truth and knowledge and science who generally kept the distinction in mind between truth or fact on the one hand, and knowledge or evidence on the other, the running together of which underwrote the arguments of the post-modernists. Trump and his mode of operation aren?t new, as Professor Kingwell recognizes. , What is new is the inability of most of the academy to distinguish in any systematic and coherent way, or want to do so, at least outside analytic philosophy departments, between what it is politically useful or appropriate to believe and what it is reasonable to believe on the evidence to be true,, and this inability has been conveyed to generations of students. . Appeals nowadays by most of the academic left to science or evidence based judgement are as a result, really quite hilarious, and, unsurprisingly, really quite futile except in so far as they reinforce what is already believed.

The devil is in the details alright, and the biggest detail is how to claw back the benefits once the recipient starts employment and is earning income themselves. The problem with welfare now is the clawback rate, in combination with the lowest marginal tax rates can still add up to a combined marginal rate of 80%, completely discouraging recipients from seeking employment. The way to counter this is to make the program a negative tax, rather than just another form of welfare. The only way to do this without discouraging employment is to ensure that the clawback rate is no more than the lowest marginal tax rate. But wait, 75% of 22,000 is 16,500, and clawing that back at 20% (roughly the lowest marginal tax rate, combined federal and provincial) means that it doesn't get completely clawed back until income hits 82,500 (16,500/20%)! By which point the marginal tax rate is 30%. So now, you have to use 30% as a clawback rate and the 16,500 is fully clawback back at 55,000 (16,500/30%).i.e. 55,000 is the breakeven point and everybody making less than 55,000 will be getting some amount of this negative tax and not paying regular tax at all. I'm pretty sure that's a lot more people than necessary. The alternative requires three changes: First, reduce the maximum from 75% of the LIM (the 22,000) to a percentage equal to that lowest marginal tax rate. Second, raise the lowest marginal tax rate. Third, raise the basic personal exemption for tax purposes to the same as the LIM. Let's put some numbers to that: The LIM is already determined to be 22,000, but if we raise the lowest marginal rate to 35%, then the maximum basic income is 7,700 (22,000 x 35%) per year (642/mon.) for a single person. This seems to me to be too small an amount, but making it larger means either increasing the breakeven to more than the LIM or increasing the lowest marginal rate. If the breakeven amount (and basic personal exemption) were raised to say, 30,000 and the lowest marginal rate were left at 35%, then the maximum amount paid would be 10,500 per single (875/mon.) This increases to the basic personal amount could only be implemented if it replaced ALL other personal exemptions/credits.This would also only work for able bodied workers. Disability benefits would still have to paid for as it is done now.

Being 7 years younger than Gordie Howe growing up in Saskatoon in the 1940s, he was naturally one of my heroes. One of my favorite memories of Gordie took place in Kingston, Ontario in the fall of 1959 during an exhibition game between the Red Wings and the Kingston Frontenacs of the EPHL. One of Kingston's best players was a tough as nails guy named Reg Fleming. Eager to show his stuff, Reg decided to demonstrate his ability by tightly checking the Big Guy. He hounded Gordie with no success for the first half of the game. Then with the puck at the opposite end, Gordie circled behind the Kingston net with Reggie in hot pursuit. As they got behind the goal, Howe reached back with his stick and tucked it up one of Reg's pant legs and sent him sprawling to the ice. It was an amazingly deft move. The referee didn't see it as he was focused on the play at the other end. When Fleming continue to hound him, Gordie turned his stick over so only the tip was in contact with the puck. With the puck held that way he proceeded to skate tight circles around poor Reggie. It was only then that Reg decided to leave the Big Guy alone. Reg went on to enjoy a good NHL career but he never tried to take on Gordie again. Jim Bulger
